performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
intro: “Der Trunkene im Frühling”, marked Allegro. Keck, aber nicht zu schnell, is the fifth song of Das Lied von der Erde. In it a bird announces spring and the drinker asks for another cup. Carl Martin Öhmann sings with the Concertgebouw Orchestra under Carl Schuricht in a live performance of 1939.

sections.label: A · Allegro, trilling winds and horns
sections.mNote: Winds and horns trill and begin without the strings.

sections.label: B · The bird’s song: solo violin, flute
sections.mNote: Solo violin, flute and harp break into the drinking song.

sections.label: A′ · first tempo, harp and plucked cellos
sections.mNote: Harp arpeggios and plucked cellos restore the first tempo.

cues.title: Opening and tenor entry
cues.text: Oboes and clarinets trill above the horns, which play figures with grace notes; the strings rest. In bar 5 Öhmann enters with “Wenn nur ein Traum das Leben ist” (if life is only a dream), and asks why toil and trouble are worth the effort.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), p. 81: opening wind and brass scoring, grace notes and tenor entry in bar 5. Hans Bethge’s text; our translation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Li Bai’s poem and its translators
cues.text: The poem began as Li Bai’s “Feelings upon Awakening from Drunkenness on a Spring Day”. The Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys translated it into French as “Un jour de printemps”, Hans Heilmann put that into German, and Bethge rhymed it. The opening thought, that life is a great dream and toil pointless, comes from Li Bai.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Der Trunkene im Frühling page, prints Li Bai’s poem in translation, d’Hervey’s French, Heilmann’s German and Bethge’s version: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Trunkene.htm

cues.title: Birdsong episode
cues.text: The drinker wakes to birdsong; “Ein Vogel singt im Baum” — a bird sings in the tree. A solo violin plays above the softer orchestra, followed by the flute and then the harp. Mahler holds back the tempo here, marking it Noch ruhiger and Zurückhaltend.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 86: solo violin, flute, harp, Noch ruhiger and Zurückhaltend. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tenor’s question, Langsam
cues.text: The tenor asks whether spring has come. Under Rit. and Langsam he repeats “mir ist” before “als wie im Traum” (as though in a dream). Solo violin and harp accompany the question, with only a few low winds and strings beneath.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 87: Rit., Langsam, the tenor’s question, solo violin, harp and reduced accompaniment. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Bruno Walter, July 1908
cues.text: In July 1908, composing again with difficulty, Mahler wrote to Bruno Walter that he had lost all the clarity and reassurance he ever won and stood “vis-à-vis de rien”, face to face with nothing. His doctors had forbidden exertion. The poem calls life a dream and spring beside the point.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s Universal Edition introduction quotes the letter of 18 July 1908 and the doctors’ restrictions: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Passage in D♭ major
cues.text: The music moves to D♭ major beneath the drinker’s line, and Mahler marks the passage “Zögernd” and “Ganz langsam” (hesitant, very slow). Muted strings, bassoons and horns hold sustained chords.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 89–90: five-flat signature, Zögernd, Ganz langsam and sustained muted strings, horns and bassoons.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the first tempo
cues.text: “Ich fülle mir den Becher neu” (I fill my cup again). The first tempo returns suddenly, with harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos, and the violins have removed their mutes. The voice continues until the text reaches the appearance of the moon.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 91–92: Tempo I subito, Dämpfer ab, harp and pizzicato cellos. Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final words and A-major ending
cues.text: “Laßt mich betrunken sein!” (let me be drunk!) With these final words Öhmann dismisses the bird and its good news. In an A-major Allegro, woodwind runs pass over string chords, and triangle and trumpet join the last flourish.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 95–96, rehearsal 14: final words, Allegro and A-major orchestral ending. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Solo violin and winds at the waking
transitions.from: A · Allegro, trilling winds and horns
transitions.to: B · The bird’s song: solo violin, flute
transitions.how: The drinker’s sleep gives way to a solo violin and quiet wind figures in A major. The markings Noch ruhiger and then Zurückhaltend slow the tempo of his waking question. The harp enters with soft chords as the tenor locates the bird in its tree.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 85–86: waking stanza, solo violin, harp and the two tempo markings.

transitions.title: Return to Tempo I with pizzicato cellos
transitions.from: B · The bird’s song: solo violin, flute
transitions.to: A′ · first tempo, harp and plucked cellos
transitions.how: The D♭-major pause moves on at Etwas fließender, and the strings take off their mutes. The tenor’s “Ich” leads directly into Tempo I subito, where harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos accompany the line about his freshly filled cup.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 90–91, rehearsal figures 9–10: D♭ major, Etwas fließender, Dämpfer ab and Tempo I subito.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, V. Der Trunkene im Frühling, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 81–96: wind-and-brass opening, solo violin and flute in the bird scene, harp and plucked cellos at the refilled cup.

timeline.note: Oboes and clarinets trill over horn and trumpet figures; the strings are silent.
The tenor enters over the winds and brass.
Strings join in pizzicato and arco as the tenor asks why toil and trouble.
Triangle and trumpet join the full band for “Ich trinke, bis ich nicht mehr kann”.
Solo violin and flute answer the tenor’s waking question; the harp enters as he names the bird.
Langsam: harp, solo violin and a few solo strings, with low winds beneath the tenor’s question.
When the bird answers “Ja!”, the woodwind trill and a muted trumpet, the triangle and the solo violin’s harmonics enter.
Zögernd, ganz langsam: muted strings, horns and bassoons under the tenor’s “Aus tiefstem Schauen”.
Tempo I subito: harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos as the cup is refilled.
Harp glissandi and string harmonics accompany the end of the tenor’s phrase.
Quieter again as he falls asleep: solo violin returns with winds and strings.
Woodwind runs play over string chords. Triangle and trumpet join the final flourish.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
